title: Adaptive Strategies to Biotic Stress in Qatar’s Native Flora
content: Qatar’s environment is predominantly arid to semi-arid, characterized by saline coastlines, inland sabkhas, and dry desert plains. Native plants in this region have evolved a range of adaptive mechanisms to cope with extreme environmental conditions, including high salinity, water scarcity, and intense solar radiation. This article focuses on the biotic stresses that affect these plants—such as herbivory, microbial pathogens, and interspecies competition—and explores the diverse strategies they employ to survive. Particular attention is given to the defense mechanisms adopted by native species against pathogenic microorganisms, including bacteria and fungi, through both chemical defenses (such as antimicrobial compounds and phenolics) and physical barriers (including thick cuticles, trichomes, and cell wall reinforcements). In addition to microbial resistance, native plants must also compete for limited resources—notably water, nutrients, and space—which are especially scarce in Qatar’s desert and saline ecosystems. Although sunlight is abundant, managing excessive solar exposure is another critical challenge for plant survival, influencing their growth and interactions with other organisms. These complex biotic and abiotic adaptations not only ensure the persistence of native flora but also shape the broader ecological balance and biodiversity of Qatar’s wildlife, particularly in fragile inland habitats.
